title: Day 90 · Week 12, Day 6 — Myths: the first weeks are the mother's job, fathers who take leave pay for it at work, and a newborn doesn't know who's holding them
summary: Three myths about the father's place in the first weeks. The first weeks are the mother's job: false — one breastfeeding training session for fathers raised full breastfeeding at six months from 15% to 25% (Pisacane 2005, 280 couples); newborns born by caesarean who lay skin-to-skin on their father cried less and settled sooner (Erlandsson 2007 RCT); flexible father leave in Sweden cut mothers' complications, antibiotics and anti-anxiety prescriptions; fathers' testosterone falls with fatherhood and hands-on care (Gettler 2011, n=624) and their caregiving brain tracks the hours of direct care (Abraham 2014); one father in ten is depressed in the perinatal year. Fathers who take leave pay for it at work: partly true and small — four weeks of Norwegian quota leave cut fathers' later earnings by 2.1% (Rege & Solli 2013), which the authors read as fathers doing more at home; flexibility stigma is real in experiments (Rudman & Mescher 2013); leave also goes with more stable couples and closer father–child relationships at age nine. A newborn doesn't know who's holding them: half true, wrong conclusion — newborns prefer the mother's voice and smell, not the father's voice (DeCasper & Fifer 1980; DeCasper & Prescott 1984; Macfarlane 1975), but they regulate on any warm chest, attachment to the father is built over the first year, and paternal sensitivity predicts its security (Lucassen 2011 meta-analysis, r = 0.12).
action: Ask your partner tonight: if the birth is a caesarean, or she can't hold the baby straight away for any reason, would she like you to do skin-to-skin in the meantime? If yes, add a 'Birth preferences' page to the pregnancy file and write it down: 'If mother is unable, father skin-to-skin.'
